paper_metadata.title: Prognosis of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is related to endophenotypes

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study clearly defines the target population (JME patients) and uses consecutive recruitment in a tertiary center. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are explicit, and baseline characteristics are well-described.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: All patients were followed up in the outpatient clinic of a tertiary center (Epilepsy Section, Department of Neurology and Neurosurgery, Universidade Federal de São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil).
items.reasoning: The setting and source population are clearly identified as patients from a specialized epilepsy clinic.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Consecutive patients who met clinical and EEG criteria for JME diagnosis were submitted to a video-EEG monitoring
items.reasoning: Consecutive recruitment is a high-quality sampling method that reduces selection bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While the follow-up duration is mentioned, the specific calendar years of the recruitment period are not explicitly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.evidence_snippet: Epilepsy Section, Department of Neurology and Neurosurgery, Universidade Federal de São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil
items.reasoning: The geographic and institutional setting is clearly defined.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.evidence_snippet: Inclusion criteria were: (a) unequivocal diagnosis of JME based on criteria defined in the revised Classification of Epilepsies and Epileptic Syndromes; (b) age over 12 years; (c) no evidence of neurological or intellectual deficits and (d) more than 4 years of formal education.
items.reasoning: Criteria are specific and include diagnostic standards and demographic requirements.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.evidence_snippet: Among 76 enrolled patients we kept following 65 (85.5%).
items.reasoning: A participation/retention rate of 85.5% is above the standard 80% threshold for low risk.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.evidence_snippet: Demographic and clinical data are presented in Table 1.
items.reasoning: Table 1 provides a comprehensive list of baseline characteristics including age, gender, seizure types, and psychiatric comorbidities.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study reports a high follow-up rate (85.5%) and provides specific reasons for the 11 patients lost to follow-up, minimizing the risk of attrition bias.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.evidence_snippet: Among 76 enrolled patients we kept following 65 (85.5%).
items.reasoning: The retention rate is high enough to limit bias.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.evidence_snippet: Six lost follow-up, two had non adherence to treatment, one had psychogenic non-epileptic seizures and two died from other causes than epilepsy.
items.reasoning: The authors know the reasons for dropout, implying some follow-up attempt, but the specific method of re-contacting is not detailed.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.evidence_snippet: Six lost follow-up, two had non adherence to treatment, one had psychogenic non-epileptic seizures and two died from other causes than epilepsy.
items.reasoning: Specific reasons for attrition are provided for all 11 missing patients.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not compare the baseline characteristics of those lost to follow-up versus those who completed the study.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Without a comparison table or analysis of dropouts, it is impossible to confirm if they differed systematically from the analyzed sample.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Prognostic factors (reflex traits) were measured using a standardized, objective video-EEG protocol based on established literature, ensuring high reliability.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.evidence_snippet: Reflex traits were defined as seizures and/or EEG discharges induction by eye-closure, photic stimulation, language, praxis or calculation.
items.reasoning: The prognostic factors are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.evidence_snippet: Video-EEG was recorded on a 32-channel digital equipment... The protocol and its analysis were based on those reported by Matsuoka et al. and Mayer.
items.reasoning: The use of digital video-EEG and adherence to established protocols (Matsuoka/Mayer) ensures validity.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Age at epilepsy onset (years) 13.70 ± 4.48
items.reasoning: Continuous variables like age and duration are reported with means and standard deviations.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.evidence_snippet: all patients had 30 min of awake EEG recording starting at 7 a.m. After this baseline record, patients performed habitual methods of activation
items.reasoning: The protocol was standardized for all participants.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.evidence_snippet: Consecutive patients who met clinical and EEG criteria for JME diagnosis were submitted to a video-EEG monitoring
items.reasoning: The PF measurement was part of the inclusion/baseline process for the analyzed sample.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no mention of imputation; however, the prospective nature and high completion rate suggest minimal missing PF data.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the outcome (seizure control) is defined using a validated scale, it relies on patient/family recall (seizure calendars), which is subject to recall bias, and there is no mention of blinding the outcome assessors to the PF status.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.evidence_snippet: Evaluation of seizure control was done according to Prasad et al. (2003)
items.reasoning: The study uses a specific, cited classification system for seizure control.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.evidence_snippet: Estimation of the frequency of seizures was based on the review of seizure calendars and specific questioning of the patient and family members.
items.reasoning: While seizure calendars are standard, they are subjective. There is no mention of blinding the clinicians assessing the outcome to the video-EEG (PF) results.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.evidence_snippet: Patients were followed for at least three years and classified into two groups
items.reasoning: The follow-up and classification method were applied consistently to the cohort.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study measures several important confounders (age, duration, psychiatric status) and uses multivariable-like comparisons, but it does not perform a formal multivariable regression analysis to adjust for all factors simultaneously.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.evidence_snippet: Patients also had psychiatric interviews... using two structured questionnaires: the Schedule Clinical Interview for DSM-IV
items.reasoning: Key confounders like psychiatric comorbidities, age of onset, and treatment (AEDs) were measured.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.evidence_snippet: Axis I refers to the evaluation of most psychiatric diseases... while Axis II refers to the evaluation of all types of personality disorders.
items.reasoning: Confounders like psychiatric disorders are clearly defined using DSM-IV criteria.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.evidence_snippet: psychiatric interviews... by the same psychiatrist (G.M.A.F.) using two structured questionnaires
items.reasoning: The use of a single psychiatrist and structured SCID interviews ensures reliability.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.evidence_snippet: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.reasoning: All patients underwent the same psychiatric and clinical evaluation.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation methods described.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.evidence_snippet: Fisher's exact test for categorical and Student's t-test for continuous variables were applied for group comparisons.
items.reasoning: The study uses univariable comparisons between groups. It does not use multivariable modeling (e.g., Cox or Logistic regression) to adjust for multiple confounders simultaneously.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no evidence of multivariable adjustment in the statistical section.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods are appropriate for the descriptive and comparative goals of the study. Results are reported transparently for all pre-specified variables.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.evidence_snippet: Fisher's exact test for categorical and Student's t-test for continuous variables were applied for group comparisons. A p value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
items.reasoning: The analytical strategy is clearly stated.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.evidence_snippet: In a first analysis patients were followed for at least three years and classified into two groups... In a second analysis we compared those completely seizure-free
items.reasoning: The strategy is based on clinical relevance (seizure freedom), though no complex modeling was performed.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Statistical analysis was performed using computer softwares SPSS for Windows release 10.0.1
items.reasoning: The tests used (t-test, Fisher's) are appropriate for comparing two groups.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.evidence_snippet: Results: Forty of 65 (61.5%) patients reached good seizure control... Group 2 patients had longer epilepsy duration...
items.reasoning: The results match the methods and all measured variables (EEG, psychiatric, clinical) are reported.
